en: Dharma Master Dao’an’s *Eulogy on the Recollection of the Buddha* Ascending the North Terrace, I traverse the perilous path;
the stone ridges are steep and the tiers are high. How many steps have I taken, walking slowly along the way?

Moss and lichen cover the ground everywhere, with only soft grasses growing there. The water of meditative concentration flows secretly, three times inverting the camels’ humps within a single li. The wind from Luo-tuo-wo [Lauterbach] blows.

Waveringly they come and go on patrol; one must still have a fine body and mind. Even an Arhat at Yan’ou Peak—how could he dare linger long? Who else possesses such mastery as the Dragon King? (The Fifth Stanza)

Ascending the eastern terrace, I passed by the Big Dipper and gazed upon the sea, where dragon deities battled; rain and hail mingled together, startling the forests and thickets as mists rolled away and clouds dispersed, manifesting a thousand transformations. Auspicious sounds resounded with the lion’s roar, causing those who heard it to doubt and flee in fear from the banquet hall. Yet, with but three or five recitations of Mañjuśrī’s name, the Great Sage, out of compassion and through skillful means, secretly manifested his presence to save them.

The Great Sage Hall is no ordinary place; dragons and fish-coils flank it on both sides. Towers lean against one another, steep and towering; once completed at dawn, the flowers and trees are already fragrant. The Bodhisattvas manifest many spiritual wonders, their faces compassionate and hearts joyful, marked by the seal of bliss. Jade-like true monks often come to welcome and pay homage, while auspicious radiance frequently rises from beneath the curtains. May the blessings of the Tang River endure for ten thousand ages and a thousand autumns.
